lesson.title: Deciding What the Computer Does Next
lesson.summary: Control flow is the set of rules that determine which statement in a program executes next, and understanding it is the difference between reading code as a list of instructions and reading it as a story with branches.
lesson.body:
A Python program is built out of statements, individual complete instructions like an assignment, a function call, or a print. On its own, a statement just describes one action. Control flow is the layer above that: the rules that decide which statement actually runs next, in what order, and how many times. Without any control flow structures at all, a program would simply run every statement once, top to bottom, in the exact order it was typed, and that is in fact the default behavior Python falls back to whenever nothing else overrides it.

There are three fundamental patterns that every control flow structure in every programming language is built from, and it helps to name them explicitly. Sequence is the default: one statement finishes, then the next one below it runs. Selection means the program chooses between different paths based on a condition, only running one of them, which is what if, if-else, elif, and match statements all provide in different shapes. Iteration means a block of statements runs more than once, controlled by a loop, though loops themselves are a separate topic built on these same foundations. Nearly everything else you learn about controlling a Python program is a variation or combination of these three patterns.

To see control flow in action, consider a tiny program that starts with sequential execution and then branches:

temperature = 95
print("Checking temperature...")
if temperature > 90:
    print("Heat warning issued")
print("Check complete")

The first two lines always run, in order, because there is nothing to choose between yet, that is sequence. The if line introduces selection: Python evaluates temperature > 90, finds it True since 95 is greater than 90, and so it runs the indented print statement beneath it. Had temperature been 80, that indented line would be skipped entirely, and control would jump straight to the final print. Either way, "Check complete" always prints last, because it sits outside the if block and belongs to the surrounding sequence again.

Indentation is not just a style choice in Python, it is how the language marks which statements belong to which control flow structure. The colon at the end of the if line and the four-space indent underneath it are what tell Python "this statement is part of the branch, not part of the default sequence." Other languages use braces or explicit end keywords for the same purpose, but the underlying idea, marking the boundaries of a block so the interpreter knows what to skip or repeat, is universal to control flow regardless of which syntax a language chooses.

Every control flow topic that follows, sequential execution, conditional statements, if and if-else and elif, nested conditionals, and the match statement, is really just a more specific answer to the same underlying question this concept introduces: given the current state of the program, which statement runs next? Keeping that question in mind while reading unfamiliar code is often the fastest way to understand it, since tracing control flow, rather than trying to hold every variable's value in your head at once, tells you which lines will even execute in the first place.
